tool.name: TSENAT
tool.version_command: echo $(R --version | grep version | head -n 1) && Rscript -e "library('TSENAT'); cat('TSENAT', as.character(packageVersion('TSENAT')), sep='\\n')"
tool.command:
#if str($salmon_input.input_type) == 'individual' #set $input_files = $salmon_input.salmon_files #else #set $input_files = $salmon_input.salmon_collection #end if
mkdir -p './salmon_input' && #for $f in $input_files #set $sample_id = str($f.element_identifier).replace('.sf', '') mkdir -p './salmon_input/${sample_id}' && ln -sf '${f}' './salmon_input/${sample_id}/quant.sf' && #end for
## Handle annotation file - create symlink preserving original extension #set $ann_ext = $annotation.ext ln -s '${annotation}' './annotation.${ann_ext}' && #set $annotation_path = './annotation.${ann_ext}'
Rscript '${__tool_directory__}/tsenat.R' --salmon_dir './salmon_input' --metadata '${sample_sheet}' --annotation '${annotation_path}' --sample_col '${sample_col}' --condition_col '${condition_col}' #if str($paired_design.paired) == 'yes' --subject_col '${paired_design.subject_col}' --paired #end if --control '${control}' #if str($advanced_options.enabled) == 'yes' --q_min $advanced_options.q_parameters.q_min --q_max $advanced_options.q_parameters.q_max --q_step $advanced_options.q_parameters.q_step #end if --filter_stringency '${data_filtering.filter_stringency}' #if str($normalization_options.norm) == 'true' --norm #end if #if str($data_filtering.min_tpm) != '' --min_tpm $data_filtering.min_tpm #end if #if str($data_filtering.min_isoform_abundance) != '' --min_isoform_abundance $data_filtering.min_isoform_abundance #end if #if str($normalization_options.norm_method) != 'default' --norm_method '${normalization_options.norm_method}' #end if #if str($normalization_options.pseudocount) != '' --pseudocount $normalization_options.pseudocount #end if --shrinkage '${normalization_options.shrinkage}' --min_valid_frac $normalization_options.min_valid_frac #if str($normalization_options.reference_group) != '' --reference_group '${normalization_options.reference_group}' #end if #if str($normalization_options.what_output) != 'S' --what '${normalization_options.what_output}' #end if #if str($bootstrap_options.bootstrap) == 'true' --bootstrap #end if --nboot $bootstrap_options.nboot --bootstrap_method '${bootstrap_options.bootstrap_method}' --bootstrap_ci $bootstrap_options.bootstrap_ci #if str($bootstrap_options.bootstrap_include_diagnostics) == 'true' --bootstrap_include_diagnostics #end if --sait_method '${sait_testing.sait_method}' --sait_pcorr '${sait_testing.sait_pcorr}' #if str($sait_testing.sait_method) == 'gee' and str($sait_testing.gee_conditional.show_gee) == 'yes' --corstr '${sait_testing.gee_conditional.gee_corstr}' #end if #if str($sait_testing.multicorr_method) != 'default' --multicorr '${sait_testing.multicorr_method}' #end if #if str($rank_options.configure_rank) == 'yes' --wy_randomizations $rank_options.wy_randomizations --eta2_threshold_moderate $rank_options.eta2_threshold_moderate --eta2_threshold_strong $rank_options.eta2_threshold_strong --min_nperm $rank_options.min_nperm --max_nperm $rank_options.max_nperm #end if #if str($jackknife_switching.jis_use_sait_fdr) == 'true' --sait_jis_fdr #end if #if str($jackknife_switching.jis_options.configure_jis) == 'yes' --jis_sait_p_threshold $jackknife_switching.jis_options.jis_sait_p_threshold --jis_threshold $jackknife_switching.jis_options.jis_threshold #end if --p_threshold $statistical_thresholds.p_threshold --fdr_threshold $statistical_thresholds.fdr_threshold --significance_threshold $statistical_thresholds.significance_threshold --divergence_ci $divergence_testing.divergence_ci --assumptions_checks '${qc_options.assumptions_checks}' --nthreads "\${GALAXY_SLOTS:-2}" --output_prefix 'tsenat' #if str($advanced_options.enabled) == 'yes' #if str($advanced_options.skip_unmapped) == 'true' --skip_unmapped #end if #if $advanced_options.save_intermediates --save_intermediates #end if #end if --output_dir './'

param.name: input_type
param.label: Salmon input format
param.help: Choose how to provide Salmon quantification files: individual files or a dataset collection

param.name: salmon_files
param.label: Salmon quantification files (.sf)
param.help: Select individual Salmon .sf quantification files. File names must match sample IDs in the sample sheet. Format: tab-delimited with columns: Name, Length, EffectiveLength, TPM, NumReads.

param.name: salmon_collection
param.label: Salmon dataset collection
param.help: Select a dataset collection containing Salmon .sf files. Element names must match sample IDs in the sample sheet.

param.name: sample_sheet
param.label: Sample sheet (metadata file)
param.help: Tab-separated file with sample information. Must contain columns for sample IDs, experimental conditions, and optionally subject/pairing information. See help section for format details.

param.name: annotation
param.label: Transcript annotation
param.help: GFF3 annotation file with transcript ID to gene ID mapping (e.g., GENCODE GFF3). Used to group transcripts by gene and map annotation information.

param.name: sample_col
param.label: Sample ID column
param.help: Select column containing sample identifiers. Values must match Salmon file names (element identifiers if using collection).

param.name: condition_col
param.label: Condition column
param.help: Select column containing experimental conditions/treatment groups (e.g., normal, tumor, control, treatment).

param.name: subject_col
param.label: Subject/pairing column
param.help: Select column grouping paired or repeated samples (e.g., patient ID, animal ID). Each unique value represents one subject with multiple samples.

param.name: control
param.label: Reference condition
param.help: Reference/control condition value for contrast specification. Must match a value in the condition column. Typically the untreated or normal condition.

validator.message: Only letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and dots allowed

section.name: data_filtering
section.title: Data Filtering
section.help: Remove low-abundance transcripts to reduce noise. Filtered transcripts are excluded from entropy calculation, so this directly affects which isoforms contribute to diversity estimates.

param.name: filter_stringency
param.label: Low-abundance filter stringency
param.help: Filter strategy for low-abundance transcripts. Soft: ≥25% presence in samples (preserve isoform diversity). Medium: ≥50% presence with TPM above median (balances noise reduction and diversity, recommended). Severe: ≥75% presence with high TPM (focus on abundant isoforms only). Choice affects entropy estimates: severe reduces noise but may miss rare isoforms and reduce diversity signal.

param.name: min_tpm
param.label: Minimum TPM threshold
param.help: (Optional) Minimum TPM value for transcript filtering (default: 1.0 if not specified). Transcripts with TPM < threshold in samples below min_samples are excluded. Leave empty to use default.

param.name: min_isoform_abundance
param.label: Minimum isoform abundance within gene
param.help: (Optional) Relative abundance threshold for isoforms within each gene (0-1 scale). Default: 0.05 (5%). Set to 0 to skip per-isoform filtering. For example, 0.05 means retain isoforms comprising >5% of the gene's total expression.

section.name: normalization_options
section.title: Data Normalization
section.help: Transform entropy values for cross-gene and cross-q comparability. Normalization is recommended to make entropy scores comparable across genes with different numbers of isoforms.

param.name: norm
param.label: Enable normalization
param.help: Normalize entropy estimates to [0,1] range for comparable cross-q assessment. Recommended (default: enabled) for comparing entropy across different q-values and between genes. Disable only if raw unnormalized entropy is needed.

param.name: norm_method
param.label: Normalization method
param.help: Method for normalization. Default (automatic): chooses algorithm based on data. Z-score: centered and scaled. Log odds ratio: robust ratio-based normalization. Relative reference: normalized relative to a reference group mean.

param.name: pseudocount
param.label: Pseudocount
param.help: Add pseudocount to break ties and handle zeros in sparse RNA-seq data. Leave blank (default) for no regularization (pseudocount=0), or specify a numeric value between 0-10 for fixed pseudocount. Typical values: 0.5, 1.0. To use automatic estimation based on library size, set to a very small value like 0.001. Critical for rank-based non-parametric tests which require unique orderings.

param.name: shrinkage
param.label: Shrinkage method
param.help: Shrinkage estimation for robust variance estimation. None: direct estimation. James-Stein: empirical Bayes shrinkage toward grand mean. Use James-Stein for small sample sizes or high-variance data.

param.name: min_valid_frac
param.label: Minimum valid fraction
param.help: Minimum fraction of valid (non-missing) values required to retain a transcript or gene (default: 0.75 = 75%). Transcripts with <75% valid samples are excluded due to insufficient data quality. Increase for stringent filtering; decrease to retain more transcripts.

param.name: reference_group
param.label: Reference group for normalization
param.help: Reference group identifier for 'relative_reference' normalization method. Entropy values will be normalized relative to this group's mean. If empty, uses first condition group.

validator.message: Only letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and dots allowed

param.name: what_output
param.label: Diversity output type (advanced)
param.help: Output type for diversity calculation: 'S' = entropy (default) or 'D' = diversity (Hill numbers). Most users should use default entropy ('S'). Choose 'D' only if you specifically need diversity measures.

param.name: q_min
param.label: Minimum q value
param.help: Minimum entropic index q. q=0 emphasizes rare isoforms (richness); q=1 gives Shannon entropy (balanced diversity); q→0 detects if diversity is maintained or collapsed across rare variants.

param.name: q_max
param.label: Maximum q value
param.help: Maximum entropic index q. q=2 emphasizes dominant isoforms (Simpson index); high q is robust to rare variants and detects dominance shifts. Examine q-curves showing how results change across scales.

param.name: q_step
param.label: q step size
param.help: Resolution of q-spectrum (smaller = more q-values, higher resolution curves, slower). Default 0.05 creates 41 q-values from 0 to 2. Smaller steps (e.g., 0.02) provide smoother q-curves for visualizing scale-dependent patterns.

param.name: save_intermediates
param.label: Save analysis object
param.help: Save the TSENATAnalysis object as RDS for downstream R analysis

param.name: skip_unmapped
param.label: Skip unmapped transcripts
param.help: Skip transcripts not found in the annotation file (recommended: enabled). If disabled, analysis will fail if unmapped transcripts are present in Salmon files.

section.name: statistical_thresholds
section.title: Statistical Significance Thresholds
section.help: Set the significance cutoffs applied across all downstream tests (SAIT, rank-based, and isoform switching). Lower thresholds = more stringent.

param.name: p_threshold
param.label: P-value threshold
param.help: Uncorrected p-value threshold for statistical tests. Typical: 0.05. Used before multiple testing correction in parametric (SAIT) and rank-based (ART/RT) analyses.

param.name: fdr_threshold
param.label: FDR threshold
param.help: False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjusted p-value threshold for controlling Type I error across multiple tests. Benjamini-Hochberg correction recommended. Typical: 0.05. Genes with adjusted p < FDR threshold are considered significant at specified false discovery rate.

param.name: significance_threshold
param.label: General significance threshold
param.help: General significance level applied across all statistical tests when no specific correction is specified. Typical: 0.05 (5% Type I error rate). May also apply to interaction tests (q × condition effects).

section.name: sait_testing
section.title: SAIT — Parametric Interaction Testing
section.help: Scale-Adaptive Interaction Testing: detects genes where the q × condition interaction is significant. This is the primary test for isoform complexity changes between conditions.

param.name: sait_method
param.label: SAIT fitting method
param.help: Which statistical model to use for testing q × condition interaction. GAM/GAMM (recommended): flexible, handles non-linear q-curves and both paired/unpaired designs. LMM: linear trends, interpretable coefficients. FPCA: dimensionality reduction for high-resolution q-spectra. GEE: robust to correlation misspecification. See help section below for detailed guidance on choosing.

param.name: sait_pcorr
param.label: SAIT p-value correction
param.help: Multiple testing correction method applied across all genes tested for q × condition interaction. Hochberg (recommended): step-up, more powerful than Bonferroni while controlling FWER. BH: controls FDR, best with many true positives. Bonferroni: most conservative, strict FWER. Holm: step-down, slightly more powerful than Bonferroni. See help section below for detailed guidance.

param.name: multicorr_method
param.label: Advanced multiple correction for SAIT
param.help: Advanced multiple comparison correction methods for SAIT interaction tests. Default uses primary p-value correction. Hochberg: More powerful than Bonferroni. Westfall-Young: Bootstrap-based, controls family-wise error rate. Benjamini-Yekutieli: Robust FDR control under dependence.

param.name: gee_corstr
param.label: GEE correlation structure
param.help:
How GEE models the correlation between q-values within each gene. Only applies when SAIT method = GEE.
• AR(1) — Adjacent q-values are most correlated (first-order autoregressive). Best for smooth q-spectra. Recommended default.
• Exchangeable — All q-values equally correlated. Use when q-curves show uniform correlation across the spectrum.
• Independence — No within-gene correlation assumed. Less powerful but most robust.

param.name: wy_randomizations
param.label: Westfall-Young randomizations
param.help: Number of permutations for Westfall-Young multiple testing correction (default: 500). Higher values improve statistical accuracy but increase computation time.

param.name: eta2_threshold_moderate
param.label: Moderate effect size threshold
param.help: Effect size (eta-squared) threshold for moderate effects (default: 0.01). Used to classify interaction strength: <0.01 = small, 0.01-0.1 = moderate, >0.1 = strong.

param.name: eta2_threshold_strong
param.label: Strong effect size threshold
param.help: Effect size (eta-squared) threshold for strong effects (default: 0.1). Classification: <0.01 = small, 0.01-0.1 = moderate, >0.1 = strong effects.

param.name: min_nperm
param.label: Minimum permutations
param.help: Minimum number of permutations for rank-based test (default: 100). Lower bound for adaptive permutation testing.

param.name: max_nperm
param.label: Maximum permutations
param.help: Maximum number of permutations for rank-based test (default: 10000). Upper bound for adaptive permutation testing.

section.name: jackknife_switching
section.title: Jackknife Isoform Switching (JIS) Detection
section.help: Identifies individual transcripts whose inclusion/exclusion drives the observed entropy changes. Uses leave-one-out jackknife to quantify each isoform's influence on gene-level diversity.

param.name: jis_use_sait_fdr
param.label: Use SAIT FDR for jackknife switching detection
param.help: Use SAIT FDR threshold to filter genes before jackknife isoform switching analysis. Enables two-stage approach: (1) identify genes with significant q × condition interaction, (2) detect transcripts with robust switching patterns within those genes. Recommended for specificity.

param.name: jis_sait_p_threshold
param.label: JIS SAIT p-value threshold
param.help: P-value threshold for filtering genes in JIS analysis via SAIT results (default: 0.05). Genes with uncorrected p-values below this threshold are included in jackknife switching detection. Lower values (e.g., 0.01) increase stringency.

param.name: jis_threshold
param.label: JIS outlier percentile threshold
param.help: Percentile threshold for outlier detection on isoform relative influences (default: 90). Isoforms with influence above this percentile are considered influential for switching detection. Higher values (e.g., 95) focus on strongly influential isoforms.

section.name: divergence_testing
section.title: Divergence Analysis
section.help: Computes Tsallis divergence — an information-theoretic measure of how different the isoform distributions are between conditions. Complements the interaction tests with effect magnitude estimates.

param.name: divergence_ci
param.label: Divergence CI level
param.help: Confidence level for Tsallis divergence estimates measuring information-theoretic distance between conditions (default: 0.95 = 95% CI). Divergence measures scale-dependent differences in isoform complexity between groups.

section.name: qc_options
section.title: Quality Control and Assumptions
section.help: Validate statistical assumptions and assess data quality. Assumptions checks verify that the chosen statistical methods are appropriate for your data.

param.name: assumptions_checks
param.label: Assumptions checks
param.help: Which statistical assumptions to validate. 'All' runs all checks (recommended). 'Essential' runs only critical checks (normality, variance homogeneity). 'None' skips validation (not recommended for publication).

section.name: bootstrap_options
section.title: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section.help: Adds non-parametric uncertainty quantification via resampling. Enabling bootstrap provides confidence intervals for entropy estimates but increases runtime ~nboot-fold.

param.name: bootstrap
param.label: Enable bootstrap
param.help: Enable bootstrap resampling to compute robust confidence intervals for entropy estimates. Adds computational cost but provides non-parametric uncertainty quantification. Recommended for small sample sizes or non-normal data.

param.name: nboot
param.label: Bootstrap replicates
param.help: Number of bootstrap resampling iterations (default: 1000). Larger values (e.g., 5000) improve CI precision but increase runtime. Use ≥1000 for final analyses; 100-500 for exploratory work.

param.name: bootstrap_method
param.label: Bootstrap method
param.help: Bootstrap CI method. Percentile: simple, fast, less accurate for skewed distributions. BCa: bias-corrected and accelerated, more accurate and recommended for entropy estimates which may be skewed.

param.name: bootstrap_ci
param.label: Bootstrap CI level
param.help: Confidence level for CIs (0.95 = 95% CI). Narrower intervals (e.g., 0.90) are easier to achieve; wider intervals (e.g., 0.99) provide stronger confidence.

param.name: bootstrap_include_diagnostics
param.label: Include bootstrap diagnostics
param.help: Save bootstrap diagnostics including convergence checks, variance ratios, and CI coverage validations. Useful for assessing bootstrap stability and data quality.

data.name: srh_results
data.label: TSENAT on ${on_string}: Aligned Rank Transform test

data.name: divergence_spectrum_plot_top
data.label: TSENAT on ${on_string}: Top genes divergence spectrum

tool.help:
.. class:: infomark
**Purpose**
TSENAT (Tsallis Entropy Analysis Toolbox) quantifies isoform-usage complexity in RNA-seq data using Tsallis entropy, detecting coordinate isoform switching and splicing-driven complexity changes that standard differential expression tools (DESeq2, edgeR) miss. While traditional RNA-seq analysis measures transcript abundance changes, TSENAT measures the **diversity** of isoform distributions (entropy) at the gene level, revealing genes with coordinated or antagonistic isoform patterns and scale-dependent complexity changes across different conditions.
-----
.. class:: infomark
**Key Concept: Tsallis Entropy and Scale-Dependent Complexity**
Tsallis entropy uses a tuning parameter **q** (entropic index) that reveals scale-dependent complexity:
- **q = 0.5**: Focuses on rare isoforms (sensitive to low-abundance variants and isoform richness) - **q = 1.0**: Shannon entropy (balanced view across all isoforms, standard diversity measure) - **q = 2.0**: Focuses on dominant isoforms (Simpson index, sensitive to major isoform changes)
TSENAT computes a *spectrum* of entropy values (sweeping q from 0 to 2+) to characterize the full complexity landscape, enabling you to identify scale-dependent patterns where complexity changes are visible at some q-values but not others.
-----
.. class:: infomark
**Analysis Workflow**
TSENAT executes a comprehensive analysis pipeline:
- **Data Filtering**: Remove low-abundance transcripts based on stringency level (soft, medium, or severe) - **Diversity Calculation**: Compute Tsallis entropy across q-spectrum for each gene and condition - **Q-spectrum Visualization**: Plot diversity q-curves showing complexity patterns across q-values - **SAIT Parametric Testing**: Fit Scale-Adaptive Interaction Testing models (GAM, LMM, FPCA, or GEE) for q × condition effects (see SAIT Method Selection below) - **Jackknife Isoform Switching**: Detect transcript-level switching patterns with jackknife resampling validation - **Rank-based Testing**: Aligned Rank Transform (ART/Conover-Iman) non-parametric test for q × condition interaction with Westfall-Young correction - **Divergence Analysis**: Compute Tsallis divergence measuring information-theoretic distance between conditions - **Concordance Analysis**: Compare parametric (SAIT) vs non-parametric (ART) test agreement - **Quality Control**: M-estimator sample influence assessment (runs automatically) and statistical assumptions validation - **Visualization**: Comprehensive plots including influence heatmaps, top transcripts patterns, and divergence distributions
-----
.. class:: infomark
**Input: Sample Sheet (Metadata File)**
TSENAT requires a tab-delimited sample sheet file containing sample information. You will provide this file and then select which columns correspond to sample IDs, experimental conditions, and pairing information (if applicable).
**File Format:**
The sample sheet should be a tab-separated text file with:
**Required columns:**
- A column for sample IDs (must match Salmon quantification file names exactly, case-sensitive, without .sf extension) - A column for experimental conditions/treatment groups (e.g., normal, tumor, control, treatment)
**Optional column:**
- A column for pairing/subject information (if using paired/repeated-measures designs; e.g., patient ID, animal ID)
**Column names are flexible** - you will select which column plays which role when you set up the tool parameters.
**Example sample sheet:**
sample condition paired_samples SRR14800481 normal A SRR14800480 normal B SRR14800479 tumor A SRR14800478 tumor B SRR14800485 normal C SRR14800486 tumor C
**Usage Instructions:**
1. Upload your sample sheet file with sample information 2. Select which column contains sample IDs (must match Salmon file names) 3. Select which column contains experimental conditions 4. If using paired design, select which column identifies paired samples
**Important:**
- Sample IDs in your selected column must match Salmon file names exactly (case-sensitive) - If sample names don't match, the tool will report a "Sample name mismatch" error - For paired sample analysis, each unique value in the pairing column should represent one subject/pair with multiple samples
-----
.. class:: infomark
**SAIT Method Selection: Detailed Guidance**
SAIT (Scale-Adaptive Interaction Testing) fits a statistical model testing for a q × condition interaction, i.e., whether the entropy q-curve changes shape between experimental conditions. The four available methods differ in flexibility, assumptions, and computational cost:
**GAM/GAMM — Generalized Additive (Mixed) Model (recommended default)**
- *What it does*: Fits a flexible semi-parametric model using penalized spline smooths for the q-spectrum. For paired/repeated-measures designs, automatically switches to GAMM with an AR(1) correlation structure within subjects. - *Best for*: Most datasets. Non-linear q-curves where the entropy-vs-q relationship is smooth but not necessarily linear. Handles both paired and unpaired designs seamlessly. - *Limitations*: Slightly higher computational cost than LMM for very large gene counts (thousands of genes). Convergence can fail with very few q-values (<10). - *When to choose*: This is the recommended default for nearly all analyses. Use unless you have a specific reason to choose another method.
**LMM — Linear Mixed Model**
- *What it does*: Fits a linear mixed model with AR(1) correlation structure within subjects (paired) or a standard linear model (unpaired). Models the q × condition interaction as a linear term, treating q as a continuous predictor. - *Best for*: Repeated measures and paired designs where the entropy-vs-q relationship is approximately linear. More interpretable coefficients (slope estimates with confidence intervals). - *Limitations*: Cannot capture non-linear q-curve patterns (e.g., U-shaped or S-shaped entropy profiles). May miss effects that are only present at specific q ranges. - *When to choose*: When you expect linear trends in entropy across q-values, or when you need easily interpretable effect size estimates (slope differences between conditions).
**FPCA — Functional Principal Component Analysis**
- *What it does*: Reduces the dimensionality of the q-spectrum by extracting the dominant modes of variation (functional principal components). Then tests whether these principal component scores differ between conditions. - *Best for*: Very high-resolution q-spectra (e.g., >100 q-values) where traditional models may struggle with collinearity. Captures the major diversity patterns while discarding noise. - *Limitations*: Less interpretable than GAM or LMM — the principal components are abstract functions rather than direct entropy values. May miss subtle effects that don't align with the dominant modes of variation. - *When to choose*: When you have a very fine q-grid (q_step < 0.02) generating hundreds of q-values, or when you specifically want to identify the dominant patterns of isoform complexity variation.
**GEE — Generalized Estimating Equations**
- *What it does*: Fits a marginal model using GEE with a user-specified working correlation structure. Uses robust (sandwich) standard errors that remain valid even if the correlation structure is misspecified. - *Best for*: When you're unsure about the correct within-gene correlation pattern, or when you want robust inference that doesn't depend on correctly specifying the correlation model. - *Limitations*: Less efficient than GAMM or LMM when the correlation structure is correctly specified. Does not model subject-level random effects, so may lose power for paired designs with strong subject effects. - *When to choose*: When robustness to correlation misspecification is prioritized over statistical efficiency. Configure the working correlation structure via the GEE options (default: AR(1)).
**Choosing a method — decision guide:**
1. For most analyses, start with **GAM/GAMM** (default). 2. If you expect linear entropy trends and want simple slope-based effect sizes, try **LMM**. 3. If you have very high-resolution q-spectra (>100 q-values), consider **FPCA**. 4. If you're concerned about correlation misspecification, use **GEE** with robust standard errors. 5. For publication, consider running both GAM and LMM and reporting concordance (TSENAT automatically computes SAIT-vs-ART concordance; you can also compare GAM vs LMM results manually).
-----
.. class:: infomark
**SAIT P-Value Correction: Detailed Guidance**
When testing thousands of genes simultaneously for q × condition interaction, the probability of false positives (Type I errors) increases with the number of tests. Multiple testing correction adjusts p-values to control this inflation. The four available methods differ in how they balance false positive control against statistical power:
**Hochberg (recommended default)**
- *What it does*: Step-up procedure that sorts raw p-values and compares each to a progressively more lenient threshold. Controls the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) — the probability of making *any* false positive among all tests. - *Best for*: Most analyses. More powerful (detects more true effects) than Bonferroni while still providing strict FWER control. The recommended default for SAIT testing. - *Limitations*: Assumes independence or positive dependence among tests. Less appropriate when p-values are negatively correlated. - *When to choose*: This is the recommended default. Use when you want strong confidence that every significant gene is a true positive.
**Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) — False Discovery Rate control**
- *What it does*: Controls the False Discovery Rate (FDR) — the expected proportion of false positives among all significant results. More lenient than FWER-controlling methods. - *Best for*: Exploratory analyses where you expect many true positives and can tolerate some false discoveries. Often preferred in genomics where follow-up validation is planned. - *Limitations*: Accepts that ~5% (at FDR=0.05) of your significant genes may be false positives. Less conservative than Hochberg, so you may get more significant genes but with lower per-gene confidence. - *When to choose*: When discovery is prioritized over strict error control, or when you plan to validate hits with orthogonal methods (e.g., RT-qPCR).
**Bonferroni**
- *What it does*: Divides the significance threshold α by the number of tests (α/n). The simplest and most conservative correction. - *Best for*: When you need the strictest possible error control and can accept reduced power. Suitable for small numbers of tests or when false positives are extremely costly. - *Limitations*: Severely reduces statistical power with large numbers of tests. With thousands of genes, the corrected threshold becomes extremely small, potentially missing real biological effects. - *When to choose*: High-confidence results where even one false positive would be problematic. Rarely recommended for genome-wide analyses.
**Holm**
- *What it does*: Step-down procedure that is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni while providing the same FWER guarantee. Rejects hypotheses sequentially from the smallest p-value upward. - *Best for*: When you want Bonferroni-level FWER control but with slightly better power. A good middle ground between Bonferroni's strictness and Hochberg's power. - *Limitations*: Still less powerful than Hochberg in most scenarios. Assumes independence or positive dependence. - *When to choose*: When you prefer Bonferroni's theoretical guarantees but want marginally better detection power.
**Choosing a correction — decision guide:**
1. For most analyses, use **Hochberg** (default). It provides strong FWER control with good power. 2. If you're doing exploratory analysis and plan follow-up validation, consider **BH** for FDR control. 3. If false positives are extremely costly and power is secondary, use **Bonferroni** or **Holm**. 4. The correction method is applied *across all genes tested*, so the effective number of tests equals the number of genes with sufficient data. 5. TSENAT also reports raw (uncorrected) p-values in the output, allowing you to apply alternative corrections downstream if desired.
